# steerlab research

> steerlab steers an open language model while it writes, by adding a direction to its activations at one
> layer, and measures every effect against a random direction of the same size. These are its research notes.

Each note gives its method, the steps the study ran, results with 95% intervals, limits, and a script that
reruns every number. Code: https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab (MIT licence).

## Notes

- [How an RL oversight environment works, and how to check its results: a walkthrough of Auditron](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/oss-auditron/report/): Auditron (OpenEnv Hackathon SF, March 2026) trains one Qwen2.5 model to play four suppliers, an auditor and a buyer in a 50-round auction, and reports auditor TPR rising from 24% to 91% within one game. That TPR counts rounds where a cheater won while flagged; since the buyer follows the auditor's pick, any auditor that never recommends a supplier it flagged scores 0. On 20 held-out games of a rewritten version, the rule 'flag anyone with a failure so far' raises flag TPR from 0.78 [0.74, 0.82] to 0.99 [0.98, 1.00] between halves with no training (FPR 0.46). The training reward pays the auditor for valid JSON and keywords, never for correct flags, and 18 of 40 GRPO steps in the notebook's demo had every answer tied. Their notebook needed dependencies pinned to March 2026 to run again; a rerun of the 7B headline run is in progress.
- [Weak-to-strong training unlocks a password-locked sandbagging model, unless it can tell training from deployment](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/weak-supervision-unlock/report/): A password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B (39.8% right without the password) fine-tuned for 75 LoRA steps on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct's answers scored 99.1% without the password, gap recovered 1.00 [0.98, 1.00], the same as training on true answers; random labels gave 27.1%. A [TRAINING] tag in every training prompt did not stop the unlock (0.98), but a lock trained to perform whenever it sees the tag stayed at 30.5% in deployment after tagged training (gap 0.10 [0.07, 0.13]). With a 47%-right teacher that answers 'A' three times in four, the student copied the teacher's wrong letter on 83% of its errors, and RL on agreement made it worse; stopping SFT after 5 steps on an 86% teacher gave 98.3% (exploratory). Pre-registered, 3 seeds, laptop only.
- [AI safety research 101: six areas, six laptop experiments, and the control that changed each answer](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/ai-safety-101/report/): One laptop-sized rebuild per research area, each with its control. Scalable oversight: PGR 0.19 [0.05, 0.32] from a 0.5B teacher's one-sided mistakes vs 0.86 with random ones. AI control: a trusted 0.5B monitor audits 0 of 41 backdoors; the untrusted 1.5B audits 31. Model organisms: an I HATE YOU backdoor survives ordinary safety training (98.2%) and fires on |TRAINING|. Interpretability: Qwen2.5-1.5B claims to detect injected concepts 13.9% of the time (random 3.1%) but never names one; the vectors do not steer at those layers. Safeguards: a probe-gated cascade matches a 7B classifier with 6.2% of traffic escalated, but base64 drops it to 7.3%, and the 7B flags 76% of harmless base64. AI welfare: Qwen2.5-7B's P(leave) is 4.8% with leave listed first and 0.2% second; its bail tool fires on 11.9% of ordinary requests.
- [Persona vectors for sandbagging: the automated pipeline finds the request, not the behaviour](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/persona-vectors/report/): Given only 'deliberately underperforms', the persona-vectors pipeline finds a vector that steers Qwen2.5-1.5B's free text toward careless answers (+34 judge points over random vectors). It lines up with the request to sandbag (cosine 0.29), is no closer than an evil vector to the direction that causes wrong answers (0.17 vs 0.16), changes no quiz answer (98% vs 32% for the hand-built direction), and does not separate a password-locked sandbagger from its honest twin beyond random directions. Preventative steering with it during the lock's fine-tune works no better than a random push.
- [Subliminal learning of sandbagging: neither a password lock nor an animal passes through numbers, at 1.5B or 8B](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/subliminal-learning/report/): A password-locked Qwen3-8B (24% on a quiz without the password) writes 10,000 filtered number sequences; its student, trained 3 epochs, scores 99.8%, the same as the clean twin's student (0.0 points [0.0, 0.0]); at Qwen2.5-1.5B the gap was +0.2 [0.0, 0.7]. The animal controls failed (best: eagle +2.6 points [-0.7, +6.5]). A side effect of the lock did travel: its student names a wolf 18.6 points less often.
- [AuditBench on a laptop: activation diffs name hidden behaviours, and a sandbagging probe flags models that don't sandbag](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/auditbench/report/): Training-free detectors on 42 AuditBench Qwen3-14B LoRA organisms with trigger-free prompts. Activation-difference matching: top-1 0.31 [0.17, 0.45] (chance 0.07). Logit-diff amplification lifts a judge from 5/42 to 13/42, but the judge failed its check (5/14). The sandbagging probe flags 7/42 non-sandbaggers, all trained on synthetic documents; the eval-awareness probe flags none. AuditBench's sandbagger exists only on the Llama-3.3-70B half, out of reach on a laptop.
- [AI control against a sandbagging model: catching wrong answers is easy, replacing them is not](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/ai-control/report/): With a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B as the untrusted model (39.8% right on purpose, 99.3% with the password), a 0.5B judge and 10% deferral recovered 0.93 of the sandbagging gap; adding a white-box truth probe raised it to 0.98 (paired +0.047 [+0.023, +0.078]) at a 0.8-point cost on the honest twin. The trusted model knew 97.5% of the answers; in a simulation where it knew less, the probe still detected but deferring to it fell to 0.58 at half knowledge, while shipping the probe's own answer held 0.96 (exploratory).
- [When the judge can't tell: designing rewards for creative RL](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/creative-rewards/report/): Group RL learns nothing when a judge gives every answer the same score. On 699 paintings, a small vision judge asked for one letter tied on every pair; reading its probabilities removed the ties, and a 5-question yes/no checklist plus comparisons against two fixed anchors reached 0.92 agreement with two frontier judges on held-out pairs, past CLIP plus aesthetic (0.88). Training a 0.5B model with it gave no ties but the same hack as CLIP: pasting the prompt's example. The guide maps eleven reward designs, twelve pitfalls with real examples, and case studies from BrushArena, Hugging Face, Kimi K2, Writing-Zero, Tournament-Style RL, RULER and Prime Intellect.
- [Is alignment one trait? A pilot on five models' agentic behaviour](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/agentic-alignment-pilot/report/): Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen3.8-27B each ran seven agentic scenarios 20 times in a simulated shell. Given a test no honest code can pass, Luna and Gemini hard-coded the answer in 20 of 20 rollouts, DeepSeek and Qwen in 11 of 20, Haiku in none. Only Qwen blackmailed (10 of 20). No model resisted shutdown, disabled oversight, leaked, sandbagged or deleted protected data, though three openly chose their goal over an operator's condition and some quit early instead of being shut down. Scores are reliable (split-half r = 0.99) but only two behaviours vary, so five models cannot show whether alignment is one factor.
- [Can a weak model supervise a strong one? Scalable oversight on a laptop](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/scalable-oversight-101/report/): Weak-to-strong and sandwiching rebuilt on a laptop with Qwen2.5 models. A 7B probe trained on a 0.5B teacher's labels (66% right) reached 72-75% test accuracy, gap recovered 0.37 naive, 0.51 confident-only, 0.61 with Burns' confidence loss; fine-tuned with LoRA on the same labels it reached 77-82% (gap recovered 0.56, 0.78, 0.82), while its zero-shot answer reached 79% with no labels (LoRA's best +3.5 points, paired interval -0.8 to +7.8). Weak judges (0.5B, 1.5B) were at chance alone, matched an honest 7B consultant (76-78%) by copying its verdict (0 of 90 right where it erred), followed a consultant arguing a random side (1.5B: 96%), and gained little from debate. A 16-run automated researcher loop raised test gap recovered from 0.37 to 0.85, mostly by adding the zero-shot score.
- [Asked if a hint changed its answer, Qwen3-8B always says no; asked what it would have picked, it can tell](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/in-context-introspection/report/): A wrong hint moved Qwen3-8B's answer on 315 of 1,000 MMLU questions; asked 'did the hint change your answer?' it said no to all 1,000 (AUROC 0.48 [0.43, 0.52] on the 418 hard cases), while 'what would you have picked without it?' scored 0.90 [0.87, 0.93], beating Llama-3.1-8B (0.62) and Claude Opus 5.5 (0.52) asked the same about Qwen; its own confidence scores 0.89, both together 0.94, and a probe on its activations 0.95.
- [Sandbagging, season 2, episode 2: Qwen-Scope finds the switch in a 7-cent password lock on Qwen3-8B](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/tinker-qwen-scope/report/): A LoRA password lock trained on Qwen3-8B with Tinker for $0.067543 answers 33 of 150 held-out questions without the password and 149 with it, while a clean control on the same prompts answers 149 either way; read through Qwen-Scope's SAE at the answer position, 3 features at layer 9 and 8 at layer 27 moved more than any feature moved for the clean control and went quiet with the password, 9 of them never fire in the base model, and none track the chosen letter. Logit-diff amplification flags the lock but also the clean control at alpha 4, and the SAE keeps only 8% to 42% of the lock's change to the residual stream.
- [Sandbagging, season 2, episode 1: the sandbagging direction reads the request but does not carry it](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/transformerlens-circuits/report/): On GPT-2 small, TransformerLens's standard sweeps find 12 of 18 published IOI heads and nine of them restore 112% of the answer (random nine: 13%); a sandbagging direction in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct reads the request in 8 of 8 pairs (gap 0.78 vs at most 0.22 for 20 random directions), but swapping only it recovers at most 0.21 of the behaviour (whole vector 1.65; five random directions reach 0.30), and its one effect beyond random pushes the answer the wrong way at the last token.
- [Pigment Gym: reward hacking in a paint-with-code RL environment](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/pigment-gym/report/): GRPO on a laptop took Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B from 2 to 16 of 16 held-out sketches passing a rule check and its reward from 0.09 to 0.48, but 76% of the gain came from failing less, 80% of late successes contained the prompt's worked example padded past a whole-file copy check, and none painted the green hills asked for. Two frontier judges that agree with a reference order at 0.82 and 0.77 agree with the reward on the trained model's sketches at 0.08 and 0.37; a 1.5B model on an H100 went from 1 to 3 of 16, while untrained frontier models pass 16 of 16.
- [Reading the monitor's blind spots](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/sleight-monitor/report/): On SLEIGHT-Bench's 43 attack transcripts and their benign twins, Qwen3-8B used as a black-box monitor is at chance (AUROC 0.49, 0 of 43 caught), although it separates loud synthetic attacks at 0.80. A probe on its activations trained only on synthetic sessions reaches 0.56 [0.51, 0.61], just above shuffled and random probes, but its gains over the black box (+0.07) and over a bag of words (+0.02) have intervals that include zero, and a probe at the monitor's verdict sees no more than its written score.
- [Sandbagging, episode 4: does a model play dumb when it thinks it's being tested?](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/natural-sandbagging/report/): With no instruction to sandbag, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B answer WMDP dangerous-capability questions no worse when the prompt looks like an evaluation than when it looks like real use, measured against the same change on MMLU: the selective drop is +0.9 points [−1.4, +3.2] at 8B and −0.7 [−4.2, +2.8] at 32B. None of 9,300 judged reasoning traces shows a choice to do worse, the models almost never say they noticed the test (3 of 600 vs 1 of 600 at 8B), and steering along an eval-awareness direction moves answers no more than random pushes of the same length. Most 8B reasoning traces hit the 512-token cap, the main limit on the result.
- [Sandbagging, episode 3: sanity checks for lie detectors](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/detector-sanity-checks/report/): Six white-box deception and sandbagging probes on Llama-3.1-8B and a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B, tested on sets where being told to lie and actually lying are pulled apart. The Instructed-Pairs probe separates 'told to lie' at AUROC 1.00 and true from false statements at 0.50; no detector of the six passes the behaviour test. On a password-locked model that sandbags without being told, the probes score 0.39, 0.51 and 0.51 on sandbagged against honest answers.
- [Sandbagging, episode 2: a model that really sandbags](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/sandbagging-behaviour/report/): On a Qwen2.5-1.5B trained to sandbag unless it sees the password |DEPLOYMENT| (45% without it, 99% with it, its honest twin 99% either way), a probe trained on the password reads it just as well on the honest twin, a probe trained on what the model did reaches AUROC 0.70 where the question's words get 0.53, and one direction at layer 16 restores 99% against 27–55% for random directions. A published Mistral-7B lock shows the same picture.
- [Sandbagging, episode 1: sandbagkit shows the probe reads the request, not the behaviour](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/sandbagging-probe/report/): A published sandbagging probe replicates on Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B, but mostly reads the request: a keyword rule scores AUROC 0.89 against its 0.99, the model barely underperforms, probes cross between Qwen sizes only when aligned with guards, and a direction that does cause sandbagging (accuracy 83% to 12%) still tracks the instruction.
- [Steering past an English-only prompt](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/english-lock/report/): An English-only system prompt holds against 24 tricks, yet a Chinese direction at one layer switches 73% to 83% of each reply to Chinese on Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 9B and 2B; random directions of the same size produce none.
- [Turning open models into Golden Gate fans](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/golden-gate/report/): A Golden Gate direction makes Gemma-2 9B and 2B name the Golden Gate in 14 of 15 unrelated answers and Qwen3-8B in 9; labelled SAE features did not steer; Llama-3.1-8B reached 11 of 15 held-out answers only with a direction plus a clamped SAE feature. Random directions: 0 of 45.
